title: The eight limbs (2.29)
hook: one sutra lists eight limbs of yoga, from how you treat others to absorption, and only one of them is a posture
tomorrow: Yama — non-harm, truth, non-stealing, restraint, non-grasping

segments.voice: Yesterday: aviplava. Viveka, telling the seer from the seen, held steady, like a mother who never mixes up her twins. Today, the eight limbs.

A yoga studio timetable is taped up by the front desk. Halfway down: Ashtanga, six p.m. Bring water. Expect to sweat. That class is a real modern tradition of its own. But the word on the timetable is far older than the class. It comes from a single sutra, 2.29, a list of eight words. Read the list, and something might surprise the six p.m. crowd. Of the eight, exactly one is a posture.
screen: `ASHTANGA, SIX P.M.` → `BRING WATER.` → `A LIST OF EIGHT WORDS.`

segments.voice: Ashta means eight. Anga means limb, a part of a body. Yesterday Patanjali said that by practicing the limbs of yoga, impurity dwindles and discernment shines. Today he lists them. Yama, the restraints: how you treat others. Niyama, the observances: how you treat yourself. Asana, the seat. Pranayama, working with the breath. Pratyahara, the senses drawing back. Dharana, concentration. Dhyana, meditation. And samadhi, absorption. Listen to the direction of that list. It starts outside, with other people, and moves steadily inward: your habits, your body, your breath, your senses, your attention, until only the object shines. Later, in book three, Patanjali calls the last three inner limbs, more internal than the first five. Teachers read the shape in different ways. Some hear a ladder: get the ethics right, then the body, then the mind. Others lean on the word itself. Limbs, not rungs. A child's arms and legs don't grow one after another. They grow together. The sutra doesn't settle it. What it does settle is the proportion. Ethics first, twice. Posture, one word out of eight. Meditation and absorption at the end, where the whole thing is heading. The coming days take the limbs one by one. Today, just hold the whole body of it.
screen: `ASHTA: EIGHT. ANGA: LIMB.` · `FROM OTHERS, INWARD TO ABSORPTION.` · `A LADDER, OR LIMBS GROWING TOGETHER?` · `ONE POSTURE OUT OF EIGHT.` · then, large: `ASHTANGA.`

segments.voice: Walk the eight in miniature: a moment of goodwill toward someone, contentment with this exact moment, a steady and easy seat, a slightly longer breath, sounds and sights left in the background. Then rest your attention on one point, maybe the breath at the nostrils, let it flow without breaks, and if the point fills everything, let it. If it doesn't, that's normal.
Ashtanga. The eight parts of yoga in sutra 2.29, from how you treat others all the way in to absorption.
Your line: ethics first, twice. The studio class is one limb; the sutra has eight. Day four hundred fifty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Classical yoga teaching presents the eight limbs of 2.29 as the framework of the whole practice, starting with the ethical restraints and observances, with posture and breath as preparation for meditation.

notes: Ashtanga Vinyasa as a modern style 'built in the twentieth century in Mysore' (Krishnamacharya, K. Pattabhi Jois): kept unnamed and general; confirm the framing is fair.
Sequential versus simultaneous readings of the limbs: presented as two long-standing readings without attribution; a Keeper may wish to name commentators.
Pranayama is described as 'working with the breath'; some will argue two limbs (asana, pranayama) involve the body. The 'one posture' claim is literal.
